title: "Research"

I am interested into work across all spatial scales, from mountain ranges over elevational gradients to site specific experimental settings. The questions I find most interesting tend to be ones where the obvious answer turns out to be wrong.

---

## <svg class="section-icon-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m8 3 4 8 5-5 5 15H2L8 3z"/><path d="M4.14 15.08c2.62-1.57 5.24-1.43 7.86.42 2.74 1.94 5.49 2 8.23.19"/></svg> PhD: Arctic and alpine plants in a changing environment

**Europe-wide redistributions of mountain plants during the Anthropocene**\
*University of Basel · 2022 – present*\
*Supervisors: [Prof. Sabine Rumpf](https://rumpflab.github.io) (Basel) · [Prof. John-Arvid Grytnes](https://www.uib.no/en/persons/John-Arvid.Grytnes) (Bergen)*\
*[Zurich–Basel Plant Science Center](https://www.plantscience.ch)*

Alpine plants are moving upslope. That much is well established. What is less clear is why some species move and others don't, whether the whole community shifts together or falls apart, and what actually sets the boundaries of where a plant can live. My thesis tackles these questions from three directions.

**What actually determines the range limits of alpine plants?**\
Temperature is the usual suspect, but the evidence is patchier than the textbooks suggest. A systematic review I led, published in *Ecology and Evolution* (2026), synthesised what is actually known about the biotic and abiotic factors that set elevational range limits. The answer is much messier and more interesting than "it's just too cold at the top".

**Do alpine plant communities becmome more similar and does everything happen all at once?**\
When species shift upslope at different rates, the composition of plant communities changes. While it is often assumed that the communities along the gradient become more similar it is still quite unclear how fast this process happens and which steps are involved. A chapter currently in preparation for *Journal of Vegetation Science* investigates this question further by using spatial scaling relationships and re-survey study spanning the last century. 

**Svalbard: Fieldwork on range shifts**\
As a guest PhD student at the University Centre in Svalbard ([UNIS](https://www.unis.no)) with Prof. Philipp Semenschuk, I resurveyed historical vegetation plots in the Isfjorden area — sites that were first recorded decades ago, in one of the fastest-warming places on Earth. This work was funded by an Arctic Field Grant from the Research Council of Norway (100,000 NOK).

## <i class="bi bi-droplet-fill section-icon" aria-hidden="true"></i> MSc: Where does the water come from? Quantifying water-uptake depths of plants in changing grasslands

*University of Tübingen · 2019–2021*

Grassland plants growing side by side do not all drink from the same part of the soil. Using stable water isotope mixing models, I quantified how deep different species reach for water, and whether that changes when the grassland is subjected to strong experimental drought. The short answer: belowground niche partitioning is more resilient to drought than expected. The work became a first-author paper in *Ecology* (2024).

A companion study (Kramp et al., *Ecology*, 2022) showed the other side of the coin aboveground. While the partitioning itself holds, individual plant traits do shift: from tolerating drought to avoiding it altogether.

## <svg class="section-icon-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M11 20A7 7 0 0 1 9.8 6.1C15.5 5 17 4.48 19 2c1 2 2 4.18 2 8 0 5.5-4.78 10-10 10z"/><path d="M2 21c0-3 1.85-5.36 5.08-6C9.5 14.52 12 13 13 12"/></svg> BSc: Vegetation changes along grazing gradients in drylands

*University of Tübingen · 2016–2019*

My BSc thesis looked at how the functional composition of dryland plant communities changes along gradients of grazing intensity. Less a question about individual species, more about what types of plants can persist and which traits the environment is effectively selecting for.
